source_text: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς αἰτίας λόγος, ἐὰν ἐπισκοπῶμεν πότερον ἁπλῶς καὶ μάτην γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος ἤ τινος ἕνεκεν· εἰ δέ τινος ἕνεκεν, πότερον ἐπὶ τοῦτο γενόμενον αὐτὸ τὸ ζῆν καὶ διαμένειν καθ᾿ ἣν ἐγένετο φύσιν ἢ διὰ χρείαν τινός· εἰ δὲ κατὰ χρείαν, ἤτοι τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν αὐτῷ προσηκόντων καὶ πλείονος φροντίδος ἠξιωμένων. Ὃ δὴ καὶ κοινότερον σκοποῦντες εὑρίσκομεν ὅτι πᾶς εὗ φρονῶν καὶ λογικῇ κρίσει πρὸς τὸ ποιεῖν τι κινούμενος οὐδὲν ὧν κατὰ πρόθεσιν ἐνεργεῖ ποιεῖ μάτην, ἀλλ᾿ ἤτοι τῆς ἰδίας ἕνεκεν χρήσεως ἢ διὰ Χρείαν ἄλλου τινὸς ὧν πεφρόντικεν ἢ δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ γινόμενον, ὁλκῇ τινι φυσικῇ καὶ στοργῇ πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ γένεσιν κινούμενος· οἷον (λεγέσθω γὰρ δι᾿ εἰκόνος τινός, ἵνα σαφὲς γένηται τὸ προκείμενον) ἄνθρωπος ποιεῖ μὲν οἶκον διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν χρείαν, ποιεῖ δὲ βουσὶ καὶ καμήλοις ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις ζώοις, ὧν ἐστιν ἐνδεής, τὴν ἑκάστῳ τούτων ἁρμόζουσαν σκέπην, οὐκ ἰδίας ἕνεκεν χρήσεως κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ μὲν τὸ τέλος διὰ τοῦτο, κατὰ δὲ τὸ προσεχὲς διὰ τὴν τούτων ὧν πεφρόντικεν ἐπιμέλειαν· ποιεῖται δὲ καὶ παῖδας οὔτε διὰ χρείαν ἰδίαν οὔτε δι᾿ ἕτερόν τι τῶν αὐτῷ προσηκόντων, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ τῷ εἶναί τε καὶ διαμένειν καθ᾿ ὅσον οἷόν τε τοὺς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γεννωμένους, τῇ τῶν παίδων καὶ τῶν ἐγγόνων διαδοχῇ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελευτὴν παραμυθούμενος καὶ ταύτῃ τὸ θνητὸν ἀπαθανατίζειν οἰόμενος. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὑπὸ τούτων. Ὁ μέντοι θεὸς οὔτ᾿ ἂν μάτην ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον· ἔστι γὰρ σοφός, οὐδὲν δὲ σοφίας ἔργον μάταιον· οὔτε διὰ χρείαν ἰδίαν· παντὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἀπροσδεής. Τῷ δὲ μηδενὸς δεομένῳ τὸ παράπαν οὐδὲν τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γενομένων συντελέσειεν ἄν εἰς χρείαν ἰδίαν. Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ διά τινα τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γενομένων ἔργων ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν λόγῳ καὶ κρίσει χρωμένων οὔτε τῶν μειζόνων οὔτε τῶν καταδεεστέρων γέγονεν ἢ γίνεται πρὸς ἑτέρου χρείαν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν τῶν γενομένων ζωήν τε καὶ διαμονήν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ λόγος εὑρίσκει τινὰ χρείαν τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως αἰτίαν, τῶν μὲν ἀθανάτων ἀνενδεῶν ὄντων καὶ μηδεμιᾶς μηδαμῶς παρ᾿ ἀνθρώπων συντελείας πρὸς τὸ εἷναι δεομένων, τῶν δὲ ἀλόγων ἀρχομένων κατὰ φύσιν καὶ τὰς πρὸς ὃ πέφυκεν ἕκαστον χρείας ἀνθρώποις ἀποπληρούντων, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ αὗ τούτοις χρῆσθαι πεφυκότων· θέμις γὰρ οὔτε ἦν οὔτε ἐστὶ τὸ ἄρχον καὶ ἡγεμονοῦν ὑπάγειν εἰς χρῆσιν τοῖς ἐλάττοσιν, ἢ τὸ λογικὸν ὑποτάττειν ἀλόγοις, οὖσι πρὸς τὸ ἄρχειν ἀνεπιτηδείοις. Οὐκοῦν εἰ μήτε ἀναιτίως καὶ μάτην γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος (οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένων μάταιον, κατά γε τὴν τοῦ ποιήσαντος γνώμην), μήτε χρείας ἕνεκεν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένων ποιημάτων, εὔδηλον ὅτι κατὰ μὲν τὸν πρῶτον καὶ κοινότερον λόγον δι᾿ ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς δημιουργίας θεωρουμένην ἀγαθότητα καὶ σοφίαν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατὰ δὲ τὸν προσεχέστερον τοῖς γενομένοις λόγον διὰ τὴν αὐτῶν τῶν γενομένων ζωήν, οὐκ ἐπὶ μικρὸν ἐξαπτομένην, εἶτα παντελῶς σβεννυμένην. Ἑρπετοῖς γάρ, οἶμαι, καὶ πτηνοῖς καὶ νηκτοῖς ἢ καὶ κοινότερον εἰπεῖν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀλόγοις τὴν τοιαύτην ζωὴν ἀπένειμεν ὁ θεός· τοῖς δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἀγαλματοφοροῦσι τὸν ποιητήν, νοῦν τε συνεπιφερομένοις καὶ λογικῆς κρίσεως μεμοιραμένοις, τὴν εἰς ἀεὶ διαμονὴν ἀπεκλήρωσεν ὁ ποιητής, ἵνα γινώσκοντες τὸν ἑαυτῶν ποιητὴν καὶ τὴν τούτου δύναμίν τε καὶ σοφίαν, νόμῳ τε συνεπόμενοι καὶ δίκῃ, τούτοις συνδιαιωνίζωσιν ἀπόνως οἷς τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ἐκράτυναν ζωήν, καίπερ ἐν φθαρτοῖς καὶ γηίνοις ὄντες σώμασιν. Ὁπόσα μὲν γὰρ ἄλλου του χάριν γέγονεν, παυσαμένων ἐκείνων ὧν ἕνεκεν γέγονε, παύσεται εἰκότως καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ γενόμενα τοῦ εἶναι, καὶ οὐκ ἂν διαμένοι μάτην, ὡς ἂν μηδεμίαν ἐν τοῖς ὑπὸ θεοῦ γενομένοις τοῦ ματαίου χώραν ἔχοντος· τά γε μὴν δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι καὶ ζῆν καθὼς πέφυκε γενόμενα, ὡς αὐτῆς τῆς αἰτίας τῇ φύσει συνειλημμένης καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτὸ μόνον τὸ εἶναι θεωρουμένης, οὐδεμίαν οὐδέποτε δέξαιτ᾿ ἂν τὴν τὸ εἶναι παντελῶς ἀφανίζουσαν αἰτίαν. Ταύτης δὲ ἐν τῷ εἶναι πάντοτε θεωρουμένης, δεῖ σώζεσθαι πάντως καὶ τὸ γενόμενον ζῶον, ἐνεργοῦν τε καὶ πάσχον ἃ πέφυκεν, ἑκατέρου τούτων ἐξ ὧν γέγονε τὰ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ συνεισφέροντος, καὶ τῆς μὲν ψυχῆς οὔσης τε καὶ διαμενούσης ὁμαλῶς ἐν ᾗ γέγονε φύσει, καὶ διαπονούσης ἃ πέφυκεν (πέφυκε δὲ ταῖς τοῦ σώματος ἐπιστατεῖν ὁρμαῖς καὶ τὸ προσπίπτον ἀεὶ τοῖς προσήκουσι κρίνειν καὶ μετρεῖν κριτηρίοις καὶ μέτροις), τοῦ δὲ σώματος κινουμένου κατὰ φύσιν πρὸς ἃ πέφυκεν, καὶ τὰς ἀποκληρωθείσας αὐτῷ δεχομένου μεταβολάς, μετὰ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰς ἡλικίας ἢ κατ᾿ εἶδος ἢ μέγεθος τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Εἶδος γάρ τι μεταβολῆς, καὶ πάντων ὕστατον, ἡ ἀνάστασις ἥ τε τῶν κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον περιόντων ἔτι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολή.
pass_a_gloss: There is the argument from the cause, if we consider whether man has come to be simply and in vain or for some reason; and if for some reason, whether the fact that he lives and remains is for this purpose, according to the nature in which he was created, or due to some need; and if due to need, whether it is the need of the one who created him or of another of the things that are suitable and worthy of more care. And considering this more generally, we find that everyone who is well-minded and uses logical judgment in doing something is not doing anything in vain among the things he does intentionally, but either for his own use or due to the need of another of the things he has thought of, or due to the natural and affectionate impulse towards his own creation. For example, to speak by means of an illustration, so that the point at hand may become clear, a man makes a house for his own need, but makes a shelter for oxen and camels or other animals, of which he is in need, not for his own use, as it appears, but for the sake of the end, and in the immediate sense, for the care of those things which he has thought of; and he also begets children, not for his own need or for any other of the things that are suitable for him, but for the sake of being and remaining, insofar as possible, the ones generated by him, comforting his own death with the succession of his children and descendants, and in this way thinking to make the mortal immortal. But God did not create man in vain; for He is wise, and no work of wisdom is in vain. Nor did He create man for His own need; for He is in need of nothing. And for the one who is in need of nothing at all, nothing of the things that have come to be under Him would contribute to His own need. But neither did He create man for the sake of any of the works that have come to be under Him. For none of the things that use reason and judgment, neither the greater nor the lesser, have come to be or are for the need of another, but for the sake of their own life and remaining. For the Word does not find any need for the creation of men, since the immortal ones are in need of nothing and do not require any assistance from men, and the irrational ones start according to nature and fulfill the needs that each has according to its nature, but are not naturally suited to be used by men; for it is not right either that the ruler and leader should be subject to use by the lesser, or that the rational should be subordinate to the irrational, which are unsuitable for ruling. So if man has not come to be without cause and in vain, and not for the need of the Creator or of another of the created things, it is clear that according to the first and more general argument, God created man for his own sake and for the goodness and wisdom that is observed in all creation. And according to the more specific argument concerning the created things, for the life of the created things themselves, which is not limited to a short time, but then completely ceases to exist. For to the reptiles and birds and fish, or more generally, to all irrational animals, God has given such a life; but to those who bear the Creator Himself within them, having a mind and sharing in logical judgment, the Creator has allotted a life that remains forever, so that knowing their own Creator and His power and wisdom, they may follow the law and justice, and coexist with those who have lived a virtuous life, even though they are in perishable and earthly bodies. For the things that have come to be for the sake of something else, when those things for which they were created cease to exist, it is likely that the created things themselves will also cease to exist, and they will not remain in vain, as if there were no place for the vain among the things created by God. But the things that have come to be for the sake of existing and living, as they have been naturally created, since the cause itself is included in their nature and is observed according to their mere existence, would not accept any cause that completely destroys their existence. And since this cause is observed in their existence at all times, it is necessary to save the created living thing, which is active and passive according to its nature, with each of these things contributing from what it has come to be, and the soul existing and remaining in the nature in which it was created, and being active according to its nature (for it is natural for the soul to preside over the impulses of the body and to judge and measure what is suitable, using criteria and measures), and the body moving according to nature towards what it is natural for it, and receiving the changes allotted to it, including the resurrection, which is a kind of change and the last of all, concerning those who are still existing at that time, for the better.

choices.english: the life of the created things themselves

pass_b_english: There is an argument from causation: we ask whether man came to be simply and in vain, or for some purpose; if for a purpose, whether his living and enduring accord with the nature in which he was created, or serve some need; if a need, whether that need belongs to the Maker himself or to some other created thing that belongs to him and deserves greater care. Looking at this more generally, we find that everyone of sound mind who acts from reasoned judgment does nothing in vain among his intentional acts, but acts either for his own use, or because another creature he cares for needs him, or from a natural, affectionate impulse toward his own creation. For instance, to illustrate the point: a man builds a house for his own need, but he builds shelters for oxen, camels, or other animals he needs—not for his own use, apparently, but for their sake as an end, and immediately, for the care of those he has provided for; he also begets children, not for his own need or for any other advantage, but for the sake of being and enduring through the offspring he generates, comforting his own death by the succession of children and grandchildren, and so thinking to make the mortal immortal.

But God did not create man in vain, for He is wise, and no work of wisdom is vain. Nor did He create man for His own need; He lacks nothing at all, and for One who lacks nothing, nothing that comes to be under Him could serve His need. Neither did He create man for the sake of any other created work. No creature that uses reason and judgment—whether greater or lesser—has come to be or exists for another's need, but for its own life and endurance. The Word finds no need in the creation of men: the immortal beings lack nothing and require no help from men; the irrational beings begin by nature and fulfill the needs proper to each, yet are not constituted to be used by men. It is not fitting that the ruler and leader should be subjected to the use of inferiors, nor that the rational should be subordinated to the irrational, which are unfit to rule. Therefore, since man did not come to be without cause and in vain (for nothing God makes is vain, according to the Maker's purpose), nor for the need of the Maker or of any other created thing, it is clear that, on the first and more general account, God created man for his own sake and for the goodness and wisdom seen throughout creation; and on the account more immediately concerned with the created things, for the life of the created things themselves—not a life that flickers briefly and then is extinguished utterly.

For to reptiles, birds, fish, and in general all irrational animals, God has given such a life; but to those who bear the Maker himself as an image within them, endowed with mind and a share in rational judgment, the Maker has allotted a life that endures forever, so that, knowing their Maker and His power and wisdom, they may follow law and justice, and coexist without toil with those who have laid hold of the life that goes before, even while dwelling in perishable, earthly bodies. Whatever has come to be for the sake of something else will rightly cease to be when that something else ceases, and it will not persist in vain, as though the vain had any place among the things God has made. But what has come to be for the sake of existing and living according to its nature—since the cause is bound up with its nature and is discerned in its bare existence—will never admit a cause that utterly destroys its being. Because this cause is always present in its existence, the created living being must be preserved, acting and being acted upon as its nature ordains, each constituent contributing from its own origin: the soul existing and abiding smoothly in the nature in which it was created, and exercising its proper functions (for it is natural for the soul to govern the body's impulses and to judge and measure what is fitting by fixed standards), the body moving by nature toward its proper ends and receiving the changes allotted to it—including the resurrection, which is a kind of change, and the last of all, a change for the better of those still living at that time.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex philosophical arguments regarding causation, necessity, and the nature of human existence versus irrational animals. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between 'the Word' (ὁ λόγος) and 'the Maker' (the contextually appropriate translation for the Creator).
